309.title: Freedom (CCC 1730–1733)
309.hook: true freedom grows the more we choose the good
309.howItsDone: Catholics are taught that freedom is a gift for choosing the good, and some practice it through daily examination of conscience and small acts of self-discipline, especially in Lent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sanctifying grace: God's own life, given as a gift. Your line was free, not earned. Today, another kind of free: what people do with their own choices.

Sit someone who has never touched a piano in front of one. Are they free to play anything? In one sense, yes: nobody's stopping them, and they can press any key they like. But they can't play a single song. Now seat a pianist who has practiced every day for twenty years. Same keys, and she's free to play almost anything: Bach, jazz, a song she makes up on the spot. Which of them is freer? The Catholic Church says the pianist, and builds a whole idea of freedom on that answer.
screen: `A BEGINNER AT THE PIANO.` → `A PIANIST OF TWENTY YEARS.` → `WHICH ONE IS FREER?`

segments.voice: It starts with a gift. The Catechism opens with a line from the book of Sirach, which Catholics count as Scripture, in the Douay-Rheims: "God made man from the beginning, and left him in the hand of his own counsel." God doesn't make puppets. He makes people who can say yes or no, even to him. The Catechism describes freedom as a power, rooted in reason and will, to act or not to act, to do this or that, and so to shape your own life. People are responsible for what they freely choose. Here's the surprise: the more a person does what is good, the freer they become. Like the pianist, every good choice is practice, and practice opens up what you're able to do. A Dominican teacher named Servais Pinckaers called it freedom for excellence, next to the thinner idea of freedom as just picking between options. It runs the other way too. Jesus says in John's Gospel: "whosoever committeth sin, is the servant of sin." The Catechism calls choosing evil an abuse of freedom that leads to slavery. Watch a habit take over, the phone late at night, the drink, the lie that needs another lie, and the pattern shows: the more it's done, the less it's chosen. The same chapter holds the promise: "the truth shall make you free." Catholics don't see freedom and goodness as rivals. Goodness is what freedom is for.

segments.voice: Find one small place in your day where you usually go on autopilot: the second scroll, the sharp reply, the thing you always put off. Picture the moment, then picture choosing differently, on purpose, not because you have to but because you can. If you pray, you can ask for the grace to choose it.
Freedom. In Catholic teaching, not just picking between options, but the power to choose the good, a power that grows the more it's used.
Your line: freedom grows. Just ask the pianist at the keys. That's three hundred nine days now.

310.title: Conscience (CCC 1776–1782)
310.hook: the inner sanctuary where we are alone with God; Newman drank to conscience first
310.howItsDone: Catholics form their conscience through Scripture, prayer, the Church's teaching and advice, and some make a nightly examination of conscience, looking back over the day before sleep and before confession.

segments.voice: Yesterday, freedom: the power to choose the good, growing the more it's used. Your line was freedom grows. Today, the voice that helps you know which choice is good.

England. A former prime minister, William Gladstone, publishes a pamphlet saying Catholics can't be loyal citizens: they've handed their consciences to the pope. The answer comes from John Henry Newman, a famous convert, later a cardinal and a saint. His reply is long and careful, and near the end of one section he writes a line that is still quoted. If he ever had to bring religion into after-dinner toasts, he says, he'd drink to the pope, if you please, but "to Conscience first, and to the Pope afterwards." A cardinal, putting conscience first.

The Second Vatican Council, which the Catechism quotes, describes conscience as a person's most secret core, a sanctuary where they are alone with God, whose voice echoes in their depths. Not a committee, not the loudest opinion in the room: a place where you stand before God with no one else there. Paul says that even people who never received the law of Moses show "the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness." The Catechism says conscience is that inner law: it calls a person to love, to do good and avoid evil, and it judges particular choices, before they're made and after. Why did Newman put it first? In the same letter he calls conscience "the aboriginal Vicar of Christ": the first, original representative of Christ in every human being, older than any office. And the Catechism says a person must always follow the certain judgment of their conscience. Now the part that's easy to skip. Newman wasn't praising doing whatever you feel. Conscience has rights, he said, because it has duties. The Catechism teaches that conscience must be formed: by Scripture, prayer, advice, the Church's teaching, and honest self-examination. An unformed conscience can be wrong, and the Church says people are responsible for forming it. So conscience isn't a way around the truth. It's the place where you meet it, alone, and answer.

segments.voice: Bring one decision waiting for you into the quiet, big or small: a conversation, a purchase, how to spend tonight. Set aside what others will think and what's easiest, and ask only: what is the good thing to do here? You may not hear an answer yet; the listening is the practice, and if you pray, you can ask God for light.
Conscience. The inner sanctuary where a person is alone with God, and the judgment that calls us to do good and avoid evil, formed over a lifetime.

311.title: Mortal and venial sin (CCC 1854–1861)
311.hook: grave matter, full knowledge, full consent; lesser sins wound but don't kill love
311.howItsDone: Catholics confess mortal sins in the sacrament of reconciliation, and are encouraged to confess venial sins too; at the start of Mass, the penitential act asks forgiveness for everyday sins.

segments.voice: Yesterday, conscience: the inner sanctuary, where a person is alone with God. Your line was the inner sanctuary. Today, what that inner judge does with the choices that go wrong.

A friendship, and two ways it can go wrong. You forget their birthday. You're short with them on a bad day. You cancel plans twice. None of it is good, and all of it strains things. But the friendship survives: it's wounded, and a little apology heals it. Then something else: you betray them, knowingly, on purpose, in something that really matters. That doesn't strain the friendship. It breaks it. The Catholic Church uses exactly that difference to talk about sin. The phrase mortal sin can sound frightening. Today, what it actually means.
screen: `A FORGOTTEN BIRTHDAY.` → `A BETRAYAL, ON PURPOSE.` → `STRAINED, OR BROKEN?`

segments.voice: The First Letter of John speaks of a sin that leads to death, and sins that don't. The Church has long read this as a real difference between sins, and the Catechism names them: mortal and venial. Mortal means deadly. The Catechism says mortal sin destroys charity, the love of God, in the heart. And three conditions must all be met at once. Grave matter: something serious, the kind of thing the Ten Commandments name. Full knowledge: knowing it's seriously wrong. Deliberate consent: choosing it freely, on purpose. All three, not one or two. Venial comes from the Latin venia, pardon: forgivable. It's the forgotten birthday, the sharp word, the small dishonesty. The Catechism says venial sin wounds and weakens charity but doesn't destroy it. It still matters, because small habits can grow, but it doesn't break the friendship. Then what softens the picture, and what heals it. Ignorance you couldn't help, strong emotions, outside pressure and illness can lessen how responsible a person is, the Catechism says. And it adds a line that's easy to miss: we can judge that an act is gravely wrong, but the judgment of persons belongs to God alone. As for healing, Catholics believe even mortal sin can be forgiven, above all in confession. The distinction isn't there to make people afraid. It's there so they can tell a wound from a break, and not treat every scrape as the end of the world, or a real break as nothing.
screen: `A SIN UNTO DEATH, AND ONE NOT.` · `GRAVE, KNOWING, CHOSEN: ALL THREE.` · `VENIAL: WOUNDED, NOT DESTROYED.` · `ONLY GOD JUDGES PERSONS.` · then, large: `WOUNDS AND BREAKS.`

segments.voice: Think back over the last week and name one small thing you regret, a word, an impatience, a shortcut: wounded, not broken. Then gently ask whether there's anything heavier, something that feels like a break; if there is, don't panic, just notice it, and know that Catholics believe there's a door back. If you pray, you can ask for mercy for both.
Mortal sin. A sin that breaks the friendship with God: grave matter, chosen with full knowledge and deliberate consent. Catholics believe it can be forgiven.

312.title: The Beatitudes (Matthew 5:3–12; CCC 1716)
312.hook: blessed are the poor in spirit, the meek, the merciful
312.howItsDone: The Beatitudes are read at Mass on the feast of All Saints and on several Sundays, and many Catholics use them to examine their conscience or pray one each day of the week.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mortal sin: the difference between a wound and a break. Your line was wounds and breaks. Today, the other side of the moral life: not what breaks a person, but what makes them happy.

Scroll through any feed and you'll see who the world calls blessed. The vacation in Greece, hashtag blessed. The new house, the promotion, the perfect family photo. Now a man sits down on a hillside in Galilee, with farmers, fishermen and sick people around him, and starts a list of the blessed that sounds completely backwards. The poor. The ones who mourn. The meek. The ones who get persecuted. It's the first thing he teaches in Matthew's Sermon on the Mount, and the Catholic Church calls it the heart of his preaching.
screen: `HASHTAG BLESSED.` → `A MAN SITS DOWN ON A HILL.` → `A LIST THAT SOUNDS BACKWARDS.`

segments.voice: Beatitude comes from the Latin beatus: blessed, happy. The Greek is makarios, the deep, lasting happiness of someone whose life is going right. So each line announces: this is where happiness is. There are eight in Matthew, each with a promise. In the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." "Blessed are the meek: for they shall possess the land." And: "Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy." Then the ones who mourn, who hunger and thirst after justice, the clean of heart, the peacemakers, the persecuted. The Catechism says the Beatitudes are at the heart of Jesus's preaching, and that they paint a portrait of Jesus himself: the poor one, the meek one, the merciful one, the one who wept and was persecuted. Read them again, and you're reading his face. Why do they matter? The Catechism says every human being has a desire for happiness written in them by God, and the Beatitudes answer it. They don't say be poor and miserable. They say the happiness God offers isn't where the feed says it is: it's in an open hand, a gentle strength, a heart that forgives. And they're blessings, not commands. Jesus isn't handing out a new list of rules. He's describing the people God's kingdom belongs to, and inviting others to become like them.

segments.voice: Let the eight pass by slowly: the poor in spirit, the meek, the ones who mourn, the ones hungry for justice, the merciful, the clean of heart, the peacemakers, the persecuted. One will catch, maybe because you need mercy, or someone near you does, or a quarrel is waiting for a peacemaker; hold that one for the rest of the sit. If you pray, you can ask for that blessing.

313.title: Faith, hope and charity (CCC 1812–1829)
313.hook: three virtues given by God, and the greatest is charity
313.howItsDone: Some Catholics pray short traditional acts of faith, hope and charity, and 1 Corinthians 13 is one of the readings a couple may choose for a Catholic wedding.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Beatitudes: eight blessings that sound backwards and paint a portrait of Jesus. Your line was blessed are. Today, three words often heard at weddings.

If you've been to a wedding, you've probably heard it. Someone's cousin walks up to the lectern, a little nervous, and reads: charity is patient, is kind. Or, in other Bibles, love is patient, love is kind. Everyone nods. It sounds written for the couple. It wasn't. Paul wrote it to a church in Corinth that was fighting: over leaders, over gifts, over who was more spiritual. And he ended with three words, and a ranking. The Church has built a whole teaching on those three, and calls them different from every other virtue.
screen: `A COUSIN AT THE LECTERN.` → `WRITTEN TO A CHURCH IN A FIGHT.` → `THREE WORDS, AND A RANKING.`

segments.voice: The verse, in the Douay-Rheims: "And now there remain faith, hope, and charity, these three: but the greatest of these is charity." Why theological? Theos is Greek for God. The Catechism calls these the theological virtues because they come from God, are aimed at God, and are about God directly. Other virtues, like patience or courage, can be built by practice. These three, Catholics say, are given: poured in by God, first at baptism. A person can grow in them, but doesn't invent them. Faith is believing God and all he has revealed. Hope is desiring God's kingdom and eternal life, and trusting his promises, relying not on your own strength but on grace. Hebrews calls hope "an anchor of the soul, sure and firm." Not optimism, which depends on how things look: hope holds even when things look bad. And charity is loving God above all things, and your neighbor as yourself, for God's sake. Why is charity greatest? In the Latin Bible it's caritas, in the Greek agape: not a feeling, not a donation, but a love that wills the good of the other. Paul describes it: "Charity is patient, is kind: charity envieth not, dealeth not perversely; is not puffed up." And why it's greatest: "Charity never falleth away." Now, he says, we see through a glass in a dark manner, but then face to face. Catholics read this to mean that one day faith will become sight, hope will be fulfilled, and charity will remain.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing that feels stuck: a worry, a relationship, a situation that isn't changing. If you pray, you can hand it to God and let him hold the rope; if you don't, just hold the anchor.

314.title: The four hinges (CCC 1805–1809)
314.hook: prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance, on which a good life turns
314.howItsDone: Catholic moral teaching, from catechism classes to confession, uses the four cardinal virtues as a map of the good life, and some Catholics choose one to work on during a season like Lent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the theological virtues: faith, hope and charity, given by God. Your line was the greatest is charity. Today, four more virtues, the ones people build by practice.

Look at the nearest door. It's heavy, maybe solid wood, maybe steel. But everything it does, opening, closing, letting people in, keeping the cold out, depends on a few small pieces of metal on one side that you never look at. The hinges. Take them off and the best door in the world is just a slab leaning against a wall. The ancient world had a word for hinge, and the Church borrowed it to name four virtues. The same word turns up on men in red hats.
screen: `A HEAVY DOOR.` → `SMALL PIECES OF METAL.` → `WITHOUT THEM, A SLAB.`

segments.voice: Cardinal comes from the Latin cardo: hinge. The cardinal virtues are the four on which a good life turns, and the cardinals of the Church carry the same word. The four are old. Greek philosophers like Plato named them long before Christ. The book of Wisdom names them too, in the Douay-Rheims: "she teacheth temperance, and prudence, and justice, and fortitude." Christian writers like Ambrose and Augustine took them up, and the Church still teaches them. Prudence is practical wisdom: seeing what's actually good here, now, and the right way to do it. The Catechism calls it the charioteer of the virtues, because it steers the others. Justice is the steady will to give God and neighbor what is their due. Fortitude is courage and firmness: holding on to the good when it's hard, resisting fear, even the fear of death. Temperance is balance: enjoying good things without being ruled by them. Here's the difference from yesterday. Faith, hope and charity, Catholics say, are given. These four are human virtues, built by practice, choice by choice, like muscles, and God's grace helps them grow. Keep telling the truth when it's awkward, and you become just. Keep saying enough, and you become temperate. The door swings easier every time.

315.title: The Ten Commandments (CCC 2052–2074)
315.hook: two tablets: love of God, love of neighbor; Catholics number them as Augustine did
315.howItsDone: Catholics learn the Ten Commandments in Augustine's numbering in catechism class and often use them to examine their conscience before confession.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cardinal virtues: prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance. Your line was the hinges. Today, ten words from a mountain, and a question of counting.

Ask a room full of people to list the Ten Commandments and something funny happens. Thou shalt not kill and thou shalt not steal come fast. Then it gets vague. Someone says be nice to your parents. Someone says no idols, someone else says that's not one of them, and a friendly argument starts about what number seven is. Both sides might be right. Christians and Jews have counted the same verses in different ways for a very long time. But before the counting, there's a mountain, a people just freed from slavery, and a voice.
screen: `KILL AND STEAL COME FAST.` → `WHAT NUMBER IS SEVEN?` → `A MOUNTAIN, AND A VOICE.`

segments.voice: It begins not with a rule but with a rescue. In the Douay-Rheims, God says: "I am the Lord thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. Thou shalt not have strange gods before me." The commandments are given to people just set free, as the way to stay free. Decalogue is Greek for ten words; the Bible itself calls them the ten words, in Hebrew aseret ha-devarim. Moses comes down with two tablets of stone. The Church, following Augustine, puts three commandments on the first, about loving God: no other gods, honoring God's name, keeping the Lord's day holy. Seven go on the second, about loving neighbor: honor your parents, don't kill, don't commit adultery, don't steal, don't bear false witness, don't covet your neighbor's wife, don't covet your neighbor's goods. Asked for the greatest commandment, Jesus sums up both tablets: "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with thy whole heart," and "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." Two tablets, one love. Now the counting. Catholics and Lutherans follow Augustine: no other gods and no images as one commandment, and coveting split into two. Orthodox, Reformed and Anglican churches count images as a separate second commandment, and coveting as one. Jewish tradition counts I am the Lord thy God as the first word. The verses are the same. Each tradition counts them its own way, and none of them leaves anything out.
screen: `IT BEGINS WITH A RESCUE.` · `DECALOGUE: TEN WORDS.` · `THREE FOR GOD, SEVEN FOR NEIGHBOR.` · `SAME VERSES, COUNTED DIFFERENTLY.` · then, large: `TWO TABLETS, ONE LOVE.`

segments.voice: If you have a Bible or a phone nearby, read Exodus 20, verses 1 to 17, slowly; all seventeen take about two minutes. If you can't, walk through the ten in your head, three for God, seven for neighbor, and stop at the one that speaks to your week, without grading yourself. If you pray, you can bring that one to God.
Decalogue. Greek for ten words: the Ten Commandments given at Sinai, which Jesus summed up as love of God and love of neighbor. Today's word.
Your line: two tablets, one love. The week walked from freedom and conscience, through sin, the Beatitudes and the virtues, to the ten words. Day three hundred fifteen, and a week complete.
